items.prompt: What does underreacting mean in this unit?
choices: Letting the incident pass with no response at all
Answering in a way that is much bigger than what happened to you
Choosing a response sized to the incident
items.explanation: Underreacting is saying nothing; it signals the behaviour is free.

items.prompt: What does overreacting mean here?
choices: A response larger than the incident warrants
Saying nothing so it goes away
A short, private word after the event, said calmly and factually
items.explanation: Overreacting is out of proportion and can cost you credibility.

items.prompt: Theo shows Mia's drawing as his. What does silence teach Theo?
choices: That doing this costs him nothing
That Mia is happy to share the credit
That the teacher will fix it later
items.explanation: Silence reads as permission, not as kindness.

items.prompt: What is a calibrated confrontation?
choices: A response whose size matches the incident and its stakes
The quietest possible response, chosen to avoid any awkward conversation
The loudest response, to make the point
items.explanation: Calibrated means matched, not loudest and not safest.

items.prompt: In the demo model, where is the reputational cost lowest?
choices: Near the middle, around a calibrated intensity of 35
At total silence, where nothing at all is said to anyone
At a public blowup, where absolutely everyone hears about it
items.explanation: The curve bottoms out near 35 and rises toward both ends.

items.prompt: Mia shouts across the room that Theo is a liar. Main risk?
choices: She becomes the one who caused the scene
She gets the credit for the drawing back at once, for good
The teacher stops pinning drawings up
items.explanation: Even when right, a loud public response can make you look disproportionate.

items.prompt: Which response is usually the best first move?
choices: A calm, private, factual word
Posting about it where everyone can see
Waiting a month to see if it repeats
items.explanation: Private and factual leaves room for a correction and keeps your standing.

items.prompt: Why is the middle response not just the safest one?
choices: It is chosen by the incident's size, not by comfort
It avoids every possible awkward moment
It always involves the manager early on
items.explanation: Matched means sized to what happened, which can sometimes mean moving up.

items.prompt: Dana and Chris both keep silent about a credit mix-up in a review. Dana says nothing, Chris notices and says nothing. Two weeks later it happens again. What best explains the repeat?
choices: Silence always means the person agrees to share credit going forward
The first silence taught that the behaviour had no cost
A second incident proves the first was deliberate
Repeats happen because managers tend to ignore small matters quietly
items.explanation: Silence signals the behaviour is free, so repeating it is the cheapest option for the person doing it. It does not prove intent.
items.reference:
Three reactions to the same incident
🤐 Silence: teaches that it is free (demo cost 54 of 100)
🗣️ Matched: private and factual (demo cost near 0)
📢 Blowup: you look disproportionate (demo cost 100)
Why: the cost of a reaction rises toward both extremes, so the best response is sized to the incident, not to the feeling.
items.learnMore:
Both extremes cost you

Silence signals the behaviour is safe to repeat. A public blowup makes you the story. A calibrated response is matched to severity and stakes.

Common mistake

Believing the loudest response is the strongest one.
items.reflection: Think of a time you reacted far more or far less than the situation deserved. What were you responding to: the event or the feeling?

items.prompt: A teammate sends a company-wide email correcting a loosely worded sentence from a single stand-up. The facts in the email are correct. What is the likely cost?
choices: Credibility, because the response outweighs the incident
Nothing at all, since the facts in the email were correct and complete
Nothing at all, since email counts as a private channel for such points
A promotion, since firm replies read as leadership
items.explanation: Being factually right does not protect a disproportionate response. Observers judge the reaction against the size of what happened.

Whether the credit is restored, since only one route can ever restore it
Whether the manager was told, since both routes always require telling them
How much each reaction costs them, even though both are right
items.explanation: Accuracy is the same, so the difference is the cost of the reaction. A matched response keeps the cost low.

items.prompt: What is a one-time slip?
choices: A repeat that happens every week
A single, plausibly careless event
An event that always has bad intent
items.explanation: A slip is one event that could easily be careless.

items.prompt: What makes behaviour a pattern?
choices: It happened once in a loud room
It repeats, often toward several people
It annoyed you a lot more than you expected it to
items.explanation: Repetition is the core signal of a pattern.

items.prompt: Which two checks does warning-signs use?
choices: Volume and tone of voice used by the person
Multiplicity and duration
Seniority and department
items.explanation: How many times and over how long.

items.prompt: First time, fast meeting, plausible mix-up. Where to start?
choices: Formal escalation to HR
The lightest workable step
A public correction at once
items.explanation: A first ambiguous event starts light.

items.prompt: Mia's classmate has done this to three kids already. What changes?
choices: Nothing, since each event stands alone
You may move up the ladder sooner
You must stay silent for fairness
items.explanation: A known pattern raises the stakes and shortens the wait.

items.prompt: Does a first-time slip deserve any response?
choices: No, a first slip never matters
Yes, but a light and private one
Yes, a formal complaint every time
items.explanation: It still matters; its size should be small.

items.prompt: Which fact most suggests intent rather than a slip?
choices: He spoke very fast in a busy meeting full of people
He did it again after being told privately
He used a slightly different word than you used
items.explanation: Repeating after a clear prompt is the strongest evidence.

items.prompt: Why can one data point rarely show intent?
choices: People never act on purpose at work
A single event has many innocent explanations
Intent can only be proved in writing
items.explanation: One event is compatible with carelessness.

items.prompt: Third time this quarter the same colleague presents your work in front of the same audience. Which start fits?
choices: Let it go, since a third time proves nothing that two did not already
Private and factual, ready to move up quickly if it repeats
Formal HR complaint, since three events always require a formal channel
A public correction, since private talks failed before
items.explanation: A pattern still starts private, because it costs little and tells you how he responds, but you should expect to move up fast.
items.reference:
Slip or pattern?
1️⃣ First time, plausibly careless: lightest step
🔁 Repeated, same person or audience: move up sooner
🔍 Check multiplicity and duration (warning-signs)
Why: how often it has happened changes where you start, not whether the incident matters.
items.learnMore:
Count before you choose

One event rarely shows intent. A repeated pattern, especially one others have noticed, tells you much more. The same two checks from warning-signs apply: how many times, and over how long.

Common mistake

Treating one ambiguous event as proof of a pattern.
items.reflection: Think of someone who annoyed you once. How would you have known whether it was a slip or a habit?

items.prompt: A colleague fixes a loose phrase on the spot: 'that was Dana's fix, right?' Which reading fits?
choices: A self-corrected slip with nothing left to address
A deliberate attempt that happened to fail to land with the audience
A pattern that needs written documentation and a manager at once
A warning sign that requires bringing the manager in right now
items.explanation: Immediate self-correction leaves no uncorrected credit. Treating it as a warning sign is overreading.

One email with an unusual choice of words
A single meeting where credit happened to be split quite unevenly
Same person, repeated, others have independently noticed too
items.explanation: Repetition across incidents and across witnesses is what separates a pattern from a bad moment.

Written claims never affect where to start
Stakes are high regardless of count, so the start moves up
It forces a public reply in the same thread
items.explanation: A formal written claim to a senior audience raises the stakes even if the count is low.

items.prompt: Which rung is the usual default start?
choices: Formal escalation to HR
Looping in the manager first, before any talk at all
A private, factual conversation
items.explanation: Rung 2 is the default starting point for most real cases.

items.prompt: What is rung 1?
choices: A formal complaint to HR with all of the details attached
A public correction in the room in front of everyone there
Let it go because it is trivial or already fixed
items.explanation: Rung 1 is only for trivial or self-corrected events.

items.prompt: When do you move up a rung?
choices: When you feel more annoyed than before
When a week has passed with no talk
When the lower rung genuinely failed
items.explanation: Failure of a tried rung is the trigger.

items.prompt: What is rung 3?
choices: A skip-level meeting held with the manager's manager, with no notes taken
Doing nothing but watching them closely
A private talk plus a written record of what happened
items.explanation: Rung 3 adds contemporaneous documentation.

items.prompt: What is rung 5 reserved for?
choices: Any first-time and ambiguous incident, however small it may seem
Anything that stung when it happened, whatever its actual size
A clear, repeated or severe pattern not resolved below
items.explanation: Formal escalation is rare.

items.prompt: What happens if you skip straight to rung 4 for a first slip?
choices: You always get the credit restored
Nothing, since managers expect it
You can burn the relationship and your credibility
items.explanation: Skipping the light options is the overreaction failure.

items.prompt: The private talk was tried and failed. What next?
choices: Repeat the same talk until it works
Go back to saying nothing
Move up one rung, not repeat it
items.explanation: A tried and failed rung is not repeated unchanged.

items.prompt: Who might you loop in at rung 4?
choices: Everyone who was in the room
A random senior leader
Your manager or theirs
items.explanation: Rung 4 involves a manager.

items.prompt: A private talk got a promise to correct the record. Two weeks later he did not. Which step fits best?
choices: Repeat rung 2 again, only more firmly and with a deadline
Move to rung 4 with a dated factual note
Return to rung 1 and let it go this time, to keep the peace
Go straight to rung 5 and file a formal report with HR
items.explanation: The rung was tried and failed, so you move up one, not skip to the top and not repeat it.
items.reference:
The five rungs
1. Let it go: trivial or already fixed
2. Private, factual conversation: default start
3. Add a written record
4. Loop in a manager
5. Formal escalation: rare
Why: start on the lowest plausible rung and move up only when a rung has genuinely failed.
items.learnMore:
Climb one rung at a time

Each rung is the lightest option that has not yet been tried. A failed rung is a reason to move up, not to repeat it unchanged.

Common mistake

Jumping to a high rung for a first, ambiguous incident.
items.reflection: Think of a conflict where you jumped too high or stayed too low. Which rung would have been the right start?

items.prompt: A promotion packet is due tomorrow and your credit is missing from it. Which start fits best?
choices: A higher rung, since the stakes are too high to wait
Rung 1, since packets are routinely revised after they are submitted
Rung 1, since packets are revised later anyway
Rung 5 for every first-time error in a packet, without exception
items.explanation: The ladder says to move up when stakes are too high for a slow private process.

items.explanation: Rung 2 costs little and gives evidence that justifies moving up, which suspicion alone does not.

A public post that records the correction
Rung 2 plus a written note of what happened and when

items.explanation: Rung 3 keeps the private talk and adds documentation for later use.

items.prompt: What does non-accusatory framing describe?
choices: What happened and its effect
What the person must have intended
How the person's character looks
items.explanation: Facts and effect, not motive.

items.prompt: Which sentence is non-accusatory?
choices: "The fix came across as your work; I built it."
"You stole my credit on purpose, and everyone knows it."
"You always do this to everyone."
items.explanation: It states the event without claiming intent.

items.prompt: Why avoid assigning motive?
choices: You cannot see it, and it forces a defence
Motive never matters in any workplace situation at all
It is rude to guess at what other people were thinking
items.explanation: Motive claims invite a fight about character.

items.prompt: Does framing it neutrally mean you think it was an accident?
choices: No, you just do not need to decide first
Yes, you have already decided that it was an innocent accident
Yes, you may never suspect intent
items.explanation: Neutral wording is a tool, not a verdict.

items.prompt: What information does a neutral opening give you?
choices: How the other person responds to an easy correction
Proof that they meant to do it
A signed agreement to share credit
items.explanation: A clean fix or a defensive reply both tell you something.

items.prompt: What is a good tone for the talk?
choices: Calm and specific
Loud and public
Vague and hinting
items.explanation: Calm and specific keeps the door open.

items.prompt: Where should the talk happen?
choices: In private, with no audience
In front of the VP, right away
In a group chat for everyone
items.explanation: An audience raises the cost of backing down.

items.prompt: What should you include besides what happened?
choices: Why it matters to you
A list of past complaints
A demand for an apology
items.explanation: A concrete reason makes the ask clear.

items.prompt: Chris says 'we worked on it together.' Dana wants to keep the talk productive. Best reply?
choices: Tell him plainly that he is lying about the supposedly shared work
State what she built and why accurate credit matters to her
Drop the point entirely to avoid starting an argument in the open
Ask him to apologise in front of the whole team at the next sync
items.explanation: Staying specific and factual keeps the focus on the record rather than on his character.
items.reference:
Same event, two sentences
❌ "You took credit for my work." (assigns motive)
✅ "It came across as your work; I built it." (fact + effect)
🔍 The second also shows how he reacts
Why: describing what happened and its effect leaves room for a good-faith fix instead of a defence.
items.learnMore:

Motive is something you cannot see. Stating what was said and why it matters lets the other person respond to the record instead of defending their character.

Common mistake

Starting with an accusation you cannot prove.
items.reflection: Think of a hard message you sent. Did it describe what happened, or what you assumed the other person meant?

"Everyone saw you ignore me in that meeting, and they noticed."
items.explanation: The first states event and effect only. The others claim intent or recruit witnesses.

items.prompt: What did Dana do in the room on Friday?
choices: Corrected Chris in front of the VP and the whole room
Said nothing and noted the date and wording
Emailed the whole team that evening
items.explanation: She chose where and when to speak, not whether.

items.prompt: How did Dana invite Chris to talk?
choices: A calendar invite titled "Credit dispute" sent to him and his manager
A casual request for a few minutes, no formal invite
A message posted in the team channel for all to read
items.explanation: A low-key ask avoids signalling trouble.

items.prompt: Where did they talk?
choices: In the middle of the open office
In an empty conference room
In a call with the VP
items.explanation: No audience.

items.prompt: How did Chris first react?
choices: With an immediate apology
Defensively
With silence and no reply
items.explanation: He said they worked on it together.

items.prompt: How did Dana respond to the defence?
choices: She raised her voice
She stayed specific and factual
She dropped the topic entirely and changed the subject
items.explanation: She restated what she built.

items.prompt: What did Chris agree to?
choices: Send a written correction at once
Mention it to the VP if it came up again
Tell the whole company about it
items.explanation: A stiff, conditional promise.

items.prompt: Was Dana certain the promise would hold?
choices: Yes, completely sure
No, she left uncertain
She never thought about it
items.explanation: She had no proof yet either way.

items.prompt: Why did she prepare her opening in advance?
choices: To memorise a script to read aloud
To keep it factual under pressure
To make it sound legal
items.explanation: Prepared wording protects against heat of the moment.

items.prompt: Chris says 'I wasn't trying to cut you out.' What is Dana's best move?
choices: Insist that he did mean to cut her out and say it plainly, since he has now denied it
Acknowledge it, then restate what she built and why it matters
Agree with him and let the matter drop completely right there
Ask him to confirm the split in front of the VP right now
items.explanation: She does not argue about intent. She keeps the talk on the record and on a concrete ask.
items.reference:
Dana's Monday talk
📅 Friday: stayed quiet, noted date and wording
🤝 Monday: asked for fifteen minutes in an empty room
🧭 Opening: event + effect, no claim about intent

Dana's ladder, as it happened
1️⃣ Let it go, for now: kept the read open
